title: Where the terminology ends
source: Rector, PEN&PAD, GALEN & GRAIL, DRAFT Nov 2026, pp. 1 and 4–5, §5.2. The aside is not the draft; it is pending Erik.

steps.title: A named clinical phenomenon
steps.body: FingerPain is a class in the terminology. The definition ties a sensation to a finger. It does not say that a particular person has this pain, who recorded it, when, or how sure they were. Those are not lines in the definition.
steps.task: Read the definition and notice what it does not contain: no person, no encounter, no duration, no degree of certainty.
steps.dump: In this dump the definition is “ExternalStimulusSensation which actsOn (PainSignal which isConsequenceOf (NerveConduction which hasUniqueAssociatedDisplacement (Displacement which isDisplacementFrom Finger)))”.

steps.title: Documentation, statement, observation, situation
steps.body: The draft’s chain for a record entry is documentation of statements of observations of patient situations. To a first approximation, documentation and the statement (by whom, and so on) belong in the record. Observation and patient situation belong in the terminology, on a core ontology. FingerPain sits on the terminology side of that line: a kind of observation, not the documentation of one event. During the project the ontology stayed almost entirely in pathophysiology, which is why a sensation-and-finger class is here and a chart entry is not.
steps.task: Keep the definition in view while you read the chain. The dashed aside under the teaching point is not the draft, and it is not signed off.

quotes.text: The medical record consists of statements about what carers have heard, seen, thought and done.
Documentation of Statements of Observations of Patient Situations.
To a first approximation, Documentation (whether recorded, etc) and Statement (by whom, etc) belong in the EHR and Observation and Patient Situation in the terminology based on a core ontology.
During GALEN and PEN&PAD, the ontology was confined almost entirely to a core of pathophysiology.
